parts.problem_md:
Planets create large gravitational fields.

State what is meant by a *gravitational field*.
parts.solution_md:
A gravitational field is:

- A region / area / volume of space; **[1 mark]**
- where a <u>mass</u> experiences a <u>force</u>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
The Earth has a larger gravitational field strength than the moon.

State what is meant by *gravitational field strength*.
parts.solution_md:
Gravitational field strength is:

- The force per unit mass (on an object);** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
Saturn has a gravitational field strength of 10.5 N kg<sup>–1</sup> on its surface and a radius of 58 000 km.

(i) State the acceleration due to gravity of an object on Saturn.

[1]

(ii) Calculate the mass of Saturn.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
(i) The acceleration due to gravity on Saturn is:

- 10.5 m s<sup>–2</sup> **[1 mark]**

** **

(ii) The mass of Saturn is:

List the known quantities:

- Gravitational field strength, *g* = 10.5 N kg<sup>–1</sup>
- Radius of Saturn, *r* = 58 000 km = 58 000 × 10<sup>3</sup> m
- gravitational constant, G = 6.67 × 10<sup>–11</sup> N m<sup>2</sup> kg<sup>–2</sup>

Determine the equation for the mass of Saturn, *M:*

- $g=\frac{GM}{r^{2}}\RightarrowM=\frac{gr^{2}}{G}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the values:

- $M = \frac{10.5 \times ( 58 000 \times 10^{3} )^{2} }{6.67 \times 10^{- 11} }$ **[1 mark]**
- $M=5.296\times10^{26}=5.3\times10^{26}\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
The following text is about gravitational fields.

Complete the following sentences by crossing out the incorrect words:

A gravitational field is a region of space in which objects with **mass / charge** will experience a force.

The direction of the gravitational field is always directed **away from / towards** the centre of the mass.

Gravitational forces are **always / never **attractive.

Gravitational fields around a point mass are **uniform / radial.**
parts.solution_md:
**Each correct sentence scores ****one**** mark:**

- A gravitational field is a region of space in which objects with **mass **will experience a force; **[1 mark]**
- The direction of the gravitational field is always directed **towards** the centre of the mass; **[1 mark]**
- Gravitational forces are **always **attractive; **[1 mark]**
- Gravitational fields around a point mass are** ****radial**; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
Astronaut A travels from the Earth to the Moon.

Explain the effect on astronaut A's mass and weight.
parts.solution_md:
To explain the effect on astronaut A's mass as they travel from Earth to the moon:

- The mass of the astronaut will not change;** [1 mark]**
- Because mass is not affected by gravitational field strength;** [1 mark]**

To explain the effect on astronaut A's weight as they travel from Earth to the moon:

- The weight of the astronaut will be less on the Moon than it is on Earth; **[1 mark]**
- Because weight = mass × gravitational field strength  **OR**  $W=mg$; **[1 mark]**
- And the gravitational field strength of the Moon is less (because the Moon is less massive than Earth);** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

equations.alt: W space equals space m g

parts.problem_md:
Determine the gravitational field strength of the Moon using the following information about the astronaut.

- $F_{gEarth}=770N$
- $F_{gMoon}=128N$
parts.solution_md:
To determine the gravitational field strength of the moon:

List the known quantities:

- Weight of astronaut on Earth, $F_{gEarth}$= 770 N
- Weight of astronaut on Moon, $F_{gMoon}$= 128 N
- Gravitational field strength on Earth, $g$= 9.81 N kg<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the mass of the astronaut:

- $g=\frac{F_{g}}{m}\rightarrowm=\frac{F_{g}}{g}$  **OR**  $W=mg\rightarrowm=\frac{W}{g}$
- $m=\frac{770}{9.81}$ **[1 mark]**
- $m=78.5\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the value of $g$ on the Moon:

- $g=\frac{128}{78.5}$ **[1 mark]**
- $g = 1.63 \mathrm{N} kg^{- 1} ( 3 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.solution_md:
Suggest what this implies about the gravitational field strength on Mars:

- The gravitational field strength / *g* on Mars is greater than the gravitational field strength / *g *on the Moon; **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
The spacecraft Centurion leaves Earth for Venus to identify potential mining locations based on fluctuations in the gravitational field strength on the surface of Venus.

The Centurion sends a landing party to the surface in a shuttle. The shuttle has a mass of 3.24×10<sup>7</sup> kg when launched from the Centurion, but loses 5% of its total mass in fuel combustion due to landing. The shuttle has a weight of 270 MN when it comes to rest on the surface of Venus.

Calculate the gravitational field strength on the surface of Venus.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Initial mass of shuttle, *m* = 3.24 × 10<sup>7</sup> kg
- Mass of shuttle upon surface of Venus = 0.95*m*
- Weight of shuttle upon surface of Venus, *W* = 270 MN = 270 × 10<sup>6</sup> N

To calculate the gravitational field strength on Venus:

- Gravitational field strength, $g=\frac{F_{g}}{m}=\frac{W}{m}$
- $g = \frac{270 \times 10^{6} }{0.95 \times ( 3.24 \times 10^{7} )}$ **[1 mark]**
- $g = 8.8 \mathrm{N} kg^{- 1} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The spacecraft Centurion leaves Earth for Venus to identify potential mining locations based on fluctuations in the gravitational field strength on the surface of Venus. The Centurion sends a landing party to the surface in a shuttle. The shuttle has a mass of 3.24×10^7 kg when launched from the Centurion, but loses 5% of its total mass in fuel combustion due to landing. The shuttle has a weight of 270 MN when it comes to rest on the surface of Venus.

The landing crew collect rock samples from the landing site. When the landing crew has finished its mission, the shuttle launches to return to the Centurion. At an altitude of 250 km above the surface of Venus, the mass lost through fuel combustion is equal to the total mass of the rocks collected at the surface.

Gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between masses.

$F\propto\frac{1}{r^{2}}$

Calculate the gravitational field strength of Venus at 250 km above the surface.

The radius of Venus is 6.3 × 10<sup>6</sup> m.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Radius of Venus, $R_{V}$= 6.3 × 10<sup>6</sup> m
- Altitude = 250 km = 250 × 10<sup>3</sup> m
- Force (weight) acting on shuttle at the surface of Venus, *F*<sub>s</sub> = 270 × 10<sup>6</sup> N (from part (b))
- Mass of shuttle at altitude is equal to mass of shuttle at surface, *m*<sub>A</sub> = *m*<sub>S</sub> = 0.95*m *(from part (b))
- Initial mass of shuttle, *m* = 3.24 × 10<sup>7</sup> kg

Construct an equation to find the gravitational force on the shuttle at altitude, *F*<sub>A</sub>:

- $F\propto\frac{1}{r^{2}}$
- $\frac{F_{A}}{F_{S}}=\frac{1}{r^{2}}\div\frac{1}{R_{V}^{2}}=\frac{1}{r^{2}}\times\frac{R_{V}^{2}}{1}=\frac{R_{V}^{2}}{r^{2}}$
- $F_{A} = \frac{F_{S} ( R_{V} )^{2}}{r^{2}}$** [1 mark]**

Substitute in the known values to calculate the force on the shuttle at altitude:

- $F_{A} = \frac{( 270 \times 10^{6} ) \times ( 6.3 \times 10^{6} )^{2}}{( ( 6.3 \times 10^{6} ) + ( 250 \times 10^{3} ) )^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

  - The total *r* is the radius of Venus plus the altitude
- $F_{A}=2.49\times10^{8}N$ **OR** 249 MN **[1 mark]**

Use this value of force to calculate *g* at altitude:

- $g = \frac{ F_{g} }{m} = \frac{2.49 \times 10^{8} }{0.95 \times ( 3.24 \times 10^{7} )}$
- $g = 8.1 \mathrm{N} kg^{- 1} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]*** *

> *Remember to always do a quick sanity check on your answers. From part (c), **g** on the surface of Venus was calculated to be 8.8 N kg*<sup>*–1*</sup>*. Therefore, above its surface you would expect it to be slightly less. If you get an answer that is greater than 8.80 N kg*<sup>*–1*</sup>* or drastically less, something may have gone wrong in your calculation. *

> *A common mistake is to also use the altitude as **r** and forget to add on the radius of the planet. **r** is the total distance from the centre of Venus to the shuttle.*
